title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Garfield Twp takes 12 months to write data center rules—what it means for bills, water and farmland across Michigan.

lines.text: Good evening and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy—the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're leading with Garfield Township's decision to spend a full year drafting zoning and permitting standards for data centers.
That's a big pause in Grand Traverse County, right? What exactly are they trying to get right before anything moves forward?
Supervisors want clear limits on power demand, noise levels and water use. Residents get time to weigh effects on taxes, traffic and the local grid before any project advances.
Why a full twelve months? Is this the first township to hit the brakes this hard, or have we seen similar moves elsewhere?

It's the latest in a string of local pushbacks. Lakeshore Township just used existing zoning to block large-scale server farms near homes and wells, keeping water and noise concerns off the table for now.
And west Michigan towns are watching that language. How does the Garfield approach compare in terms of giving residents real input?

Garfield's timeline is more deliberate. It lets the township study concrete numbers on megawatts and daily water use, similar to what Mid-Michigan residents will hear at a university-hosted town hall coming up.
That town hall sounds useful. Who exactly gets to ask questions there, and what kind of data will they see?
Anyone within about thirty miles. They'll get specifics on how proposed centers could affect electricity rates and aquifer levels—real numbers, not just estimates.

Higher electric bills are the big fear for ratepayers. We heard yesterday that one utility's twenty-year plan calls for more than doubling capacity partly to serve data centers. How does that tie into these local delays?

Exactly. If projects get slowed or shaped by rules like Garfield's, it could change where and how fast that new capacity is needed. Ratepayers across the state would still foot the bill for upgrades if they move ahead.
Water is another flashpoint. Ypsilanti-area residents are planning a protest Saturday over two proposed campuses that could pull millions of gallons daily. How widespread is that concern?
Very. Lenox Township residents are also demanding full disclosure after learning about plans through back channels, worried about noise, power strain and lost farmland in Macomb County.
Transparency keeps coming up. Is that why a second recall bid failed yesterday for an official tied to a data center rezoning?

Election officials rejected it, but the underlying fight over land-use changes that could open the door to server farms is still very much alive. Voters thirty miles away are watching how these disputes play out.
Farmland is another piece. A rural property owner wants to annex into a nearby city so a data center can go on that land. What does that shift mean for the township left behind?
Tax revenue and local control move with the annexation. Residents even thirty miles away could feel changes in land use and services if it succeeds.
Ionia is also weighing whether to let data centers tap city power and land—hundreds of megawatts. Any vote yet?
No vote, but the conversation signals the city is open. Residents thirty miles away would see higher utility bills if new plants or lines are needed.
And yesterday University of Michigan's new computing center raised nuclear weapons worries. How does that fit into the bigger picture of data centers and local oversight?
Ann Arbor residents and activists want clearer answers on possible military ties. It affects state research funding and how the university expands in the area.
So across the state we're seeing everything from outright blocks to year-long studies to protests. What's the common thread for someone listening in, say, Oakland or Kent County?
Power and water demands hit ratepayers and aquifers no matter where the centers land. Local rules like Garfield's could set precedents that travel.
What happens next in Garfield specifically? Do they have a timeline for public input during those twelve months?
The supervisors said the delay itself gives locals time to weigh impacts. We'll watch for meeting notices on how residents can weigh in.
Sounds like a model other townships might copy if the data from that Mid-Michigan town hall shows big numbers.
Exactly. The conversation is just getting started.
Let's move to a few other stories that broke today and yesterday.
Mid-Michigan residents get their first detailed look at data center power and water demands at that university town hall. Concrete megawatt and daily water figures on the table.
And Lakeshore Township used existing zoning to block data centers near homes and wells—no new rules needed, just enforcement.
Ypsilanti-area activists plan a Saturday protest at the Van Buren Township line against two proposed campuses drawing millions of gallons daily.
A farm owner is pushing annexation into a nearby city to build on rural land, shifting taxes and control away from the township.
Yesterday, U-M's computing center plans drew fire over possible nuclear weapons work ties. Activists want clearer answers.
Lenox Township residents are demanding full disclosure after learning of proposals only through back channels—noise, power and farmland worries in Macomb County.
A second recall attempt failed for an official tied to data center rezoning. The land-use fight continues.
And Ionia council members discussed inviting large-scale facilities that could pull hundreds of megawatts from the local grid—no vote yet.
Finally, Michigan ratepayers face higher bills as a utility seeks to more than double capacity over twenty years, partly for data center growth.
Now, on deck for listeners who want to show up. The Mid-Michigan town hall is coming soon—check local university listings for exact time and place.
The Ypsilanti-area protest is Saturday at the Van Buren Township line. Anyone within driving distance of Washtenaw or Wayne counties has a stake.
Garfield Township meetings over the next year will be where the new zoning rules get shaped—watch township notices for dates.
Ionia council will likely revisit the power and land discussion at future sessions.
And keep an eye on annexation hearings if that rural farm proposal advances.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.
